claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native distribution and concentration of MnS inclusions in its matrix.
Prolonged annealing at approximately 750°C reduces the concentration of MnS inclusions in Q235 steel.
Prolonged annealing at approximately 750°C homogenizes the distribution of MnS inclusions in Q235 steel.
The proposed study compares annealed and untreated Q235 specimens in chloride-rich salt spray at 25°C and 60°C.
The size, distribution, and concentration of MnS inclusions govern localized corrosion behavior in Q235 steel.
MnS inclusions serve as local anodic sites in Q235 steel.
Local anodic behavior at MnS inclusions initiates galvanic corrosion.
Reducing the number of MnS inclusions decreases the number of electrochemically active sites available for chloride attack.
A more uniform MnS inclusion distribution suppresses localized corrosion, particularly pitting.
Annealed Q235 specimens will exhibit less pitting initiation than untreated specimens.
Annealed Q235 specimens will exhibit slower propagation of localized corrosion than untreated specimens.
Annealed Q235 specimens will exhibit a lower overall corrosion rate than untreated specimens.
The corrosion-suppression effect of annealing will be more pronounced at 60°C than at 25°C.
Increased chemical activity at elevated temperature causes the stronger corrosion-suppression effect.
The magnitude of corrosion suppression depends on annealing parameters and inherent variation in MnS inclusion distributions.
Changes in alloy composition or exposure severity may alter the predicted outcome.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in pitting initiation and overall corrosion rate at both temperatures would falsify the proposed MnS-governed mechanism.
